passages.t: Jerusalem a heavy stone to the nations
passages.happening:
‘This is the burden of the word of the LORD concerning Israel’ (verse 1), from the LORD who stretches out the heavens, lays the foundation of the earth and forms the human spirit. He will make Jerusalem a cup that makes the surrounding peoples stagger, when Judah and Jerusalem are besieged (verse 2). On that day, when the nations gather against her, Jerusalem will be a heavy stone; all who try to lift it will injure themselves (verse 3).

God will strike the horses with panic and the riders with madness, and keep watch over Judah (verse 4). The leaders of Judah will say that the people of Jerusalem are their strength, because the LORD is their God (verse 5). The clans of Judah will be like a firepot in a woodpile (verse 6). The LORD will save the tents of Judah first, so that the house of David will not be raised above them (verse 7). He will defend Jerusalem, so that the weakest among them will be like David (verse 8), and he will set out against the nations that come against Jerusalem (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The second collection of oracles opens here, with God named as the creator of heaven, earth and the human spirit. The one who made everything is the one who will defend his people.

A cup that makes people stagger is a common prophetic picture of God's judgment, as if the nations drank a strong wine. A heavy stone injures anyone who tries to heave it away. The pictures say that the nations who attack Jerusalem will be undone by it.

The order of rescue is pointed. The countryside of Judah is saved first, so that the royal house and the capital will not lord it over the rest. Even the weakest will be like David, and David's house will be like the angel of the LORD who went before Israel.
passages.later: Isaiah too pictured the cup of God's wrath passed to Jerusalem's enemies (Isaiah 51:22-23). The angel of God went before Israel's camp out of Egypt (Exodus 14:19).
passages.hard:
How should a chapter about nations gathered against Jerusalem and destroyed be read today?

The chapter belongs to the second collection of Zechariah's oracles, highly figurative poetry about the future, and readers disagree whether its battles refer to events after the exile, to the coming of Christ and the church, to a future restoration of Israel, or to several of these. It is God who defends his people, and it is God who acts against the nations. The chapter gives no warrant for violence against any people, and it makes no claim about any modern state, city or border.
passages.asks: God makes even the weakest like David. Ask where you feel weakest, and what it would mean for God to be your strength there. And ask whether you have looked down on anyone God promises to raise up.

passages.t: A spirit of grace, and the one they pierced
passages.happening:
‘Then I will pour out on the house of David and on the people of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and prayer, and they will look on Me, the One they have pierced’ (verse 10). They will mourn for him as for an only child and grieve bitterly as for a firstborn son.

On that day the wailing in Jerusalem will be as great as the wailing of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo (verse 11). The land will mourn, each clan on its own, their wives apart: the clan of David, the clan of Nathan, the clan of Levi, the clan of Shimei, and all the rest (verses 12-14).
passages.hearers:
The rescue of verses 1 to 9 is followed not by celebration but by grief. God pours out a spirit of grace and prayer, and the people look on the one they pierced and mourn. Mourning for an only child or a firstborn son was the deepest grief a family knew.

The mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo is a real reference whose meaning is uncertain. Many interpreters connect it with the national mourning for King Josiah, killed by Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo in 609 BC and lamented for generations. Others think Hadad-rimmon was a place near Megiddo, or the name of a storm god whose ritual mourning was well known. On either view, it names the greatest grief the land had known.

The clans mourn separately, royal and priestly houses and all the rest, husbands and wives apart, each before God.
passages.later: The singers of Judah lamented Josiah after his death at Megiddo (2 Chronicles 35:24-25). John says that when a soldier pierced Jesus' side, another Scripture said, ‘They will look on the One they have pierced’ (John 19:37), and Revelation applies the verse to his return (Revelation 1:7).
passages.hard:
Does verse 10 speak of looking on God himself or on another, and who is the pierced one?

The standard Hebrew text has the people look to the speaker, God himself, whom they pierced, and then says they will mourn for him. Some Hebrew manuscripts read to him in the first clause, and John quotes it in the third person. Many modern scholars accept the first person as the harder and better attested reading. The question is then how God can be pierced. Some interpreters take the verb figuratively, as grieving or insulting God by rejecting him. Others take the pierced one as God's representative, perhaps the rejected shepherd of chapter 11 or a martyred leader, so that piercing him is piercing God. Later Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, applied the verse to a messiah son of Joseph who would die in battle. Christians read it with John of Jesus.

This mourning is the house of David's and Jerusalem's own grief, poured out by God's grace. It is never a reason to blame the Jewish people.
passages.asks: God pours out a spirit of grace and prayer, and the people mourn for the one they pierced. Ask what it means that true grief over wrong is itself God's gift. And ask what you have wounded that you have not yet mourned.
